blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the head of a singly linked list, return `true` if it is **circular** — its last node points back to the head instead of to null — and `false` otherwise. An empty list is not circular. (A list whose last node points back into the **middle** is a different problem: Linked List Cycle.)

blocks.alt: Two lists of 1, 2, 3, 4. In the first, the last node points to null: walking from the head eventually falls off the end, so it is not circular. In the second, the last node's arrow curves back to the head: walking from the head arrives back at the head, so it is circular.

elements.text: walk from the head: null means no, back at the head means yes
elements.originalText: walk from the head: null means no, back at the head means yes

blocks.code:
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> (back to 1)    ->  true
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> null           ->  false
5 -> (back to 5)                   ->  true
empty list                         ->  false

blocks.text: A circular list has **no null to stop at**. Every algorithm on one needs a different stopping rule — usually "we're back where we started" — and that's where most circular-list bugs come from: a loop written for a normal list runs forever. The questions in this chapter all turn on that idea: detecting the ring, **using** a ring on purpose (Rotate List closes one and cuts it), keeping a ring sorted, and simulating turn-taking round a circle.

Here the stopping rule decides the answer. Walk from the head: if you reach **null**, the list has an end; if you come **back to the head**, it's circular. With the guarantee that any loop goes back to the head, one of the two must happen within n steps.
Without trusting any guarantee, keep a set of visited nodes. The first node you meet twice tells you where the loop goes; the list is circular only if that node is the head.
**Time O(n), space O(n).** It even handles a loop back into the middle (answering false), but it pays for a set as big as the list.
2. Walk until null or back at the head

blocks.caption: Two ways out of the loop: null (not circular) or the head (circular).

blocks.code:
def is_circular(head):
    if head is None:
        return False                     # an empty list has no ring
    curr = head.next
    while curr is not None and curr is not head:   # until the end, or back at the start
        curr = curr.next
    return curr is head                  # back at the head: circular; fell off at None: not

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** Starting at `head.next` matters: starting at the head itself, the loop would stop before taking a single step.

blocks.alt: Set of seen nodes: O(n) time, O(n) space. Walk to null or head: O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: If the loop could go back to **any** node, approach 2 would run forever on a list like 1 → 2 → 3 → 2. Then use Floyd's slow and fast pointers (Linked List Cycle) to find whether there's a loop at all, in O(1) space.

items: **One node pointing to itself** — true: `head.next` is the head.
**Starting the walk at `head`** — `while (curr !== head)` stops immediately; start at `head.next`.
**Linked List Cycle** — a loop that may go back to any node: Floyd's tortoise and hare. In the singly linked chapter.
**Count the nodes in a circular list** — the same walk, counting until you're back at the head.
**Split a circular list into two halves** — find the middle with slow and fast pointers, then close each half into its own ring.
